title: Tamsin and the Uniform
premise: In 1918 London, Jonah Montrose drives for suffragist Edith Fairweather and quietly reads the correspondence he carries, believing himself a spectator to history. When a sealed letter reveals a plot by government men to falsify the record of a wartime atrocity tied to Edith's brother, Jonah must choose between his invisibility—his only protection—and getting the truth into print before the armistice lets the victors bury it. Betrayed by a colleague, hunted by men who can make people disappear, and falling in love with Edith's stenographer, Clara, Jonah smuggles the evidence through a city celebrating a peace built on lies. The book ends with the letter published hours after the armistice is signed: Edith's brother is posthumously cleared, Clara and Jonah leave London together, and Jonah finally accepts that he was never a bystander at all.
about_author: Beatrix Hartwell is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing private letters from the First World War, an experience that taught her history is written by whoever keeps the paperwork. She writes from a cottage in the Cotswolds, where she still reads other people's mail—only now, with permission.

chapters.title: The Man Who Reads Other People's Mail
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. We meet him driving Edith Fairweather through a rain-soaked London, reading letters by lamplight in the garage, convinced he's a footnote to history. Emotional beat: comfortable self-erasure, with a flicker of loneliness he won't name.

chapters.title: A Letter Sealed Twice
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A letter addressed to Edith bears two seals—the inner one broken before it reached him. Inside: a reference to 'the Fairweather business at Vireaux.' Jonah delivers it unread to no one and lies to Edith for the first time. Beat: dread disguised as duty.

chapters.title: Miss Ashford Takes Shorthand
chapters.summary: Clara's POV. Clara Ashford, Edith's stenographer, notices Jonah watching her hands during dictation. They trade dry remarks about the war office's terrible handwriting. Beat: wary attraction; Clara is sharper and more suspicious than Jonah expects.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Didn't Come Home
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Edith asks Jonah to retrieve her late brother Thomas's effects from a records office. A clerk warns him off a missing file. Jonah pockets a requisition slip instead. Beat: the spectator's first small theft.

chapters.title: Vireaux
chapters.summary: Clara's POV, reading Thomas's letters aloud to Edith. His final dispatch describes an order given, then denied, then blamed on the dead. Edith goes very still. Beat: grief curdling into purpose.

chapters.title: The Men from the Ministry
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Two courteous officials visit the house asking about 'misplaced correspondence.' Jonah realizes his reading habit may be known. He returns a letter he should have kept. Beat: fear wearing the mask of professionalism.

chapters.title: What Clara Keeps in Her Desk
chapters.summary: Clara's POV. Clara reveals she's been copying Edith's sensitive correspondence for months—insurance, she calls it. She catches Jonah reading and doesn't report him; instead she tests him with a false detail. Beat: alliance formed through mutual blackmail, almost tender.

chapters.title: The Driver's Confession
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah admits to Clara he reads everything, has for years. She calls him a coward and a witness in the same breath. Beat: shame and relief entangled; first real intimacy.

chapters.title: An Offer of Invisibility
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The ministry men offer Jonah money to report on Edith's 'unstable' correspondence. He accepts, planning to feed them nothing. Beat: the terrible arithmetic of survival—he has become a double agent in his own kitchen.

chapters.title: The Armistice Rumor
chapters.summary: Clara's POV. Peace feels close; the papers smell of celebration. Edith announces she'll publish Thomas's letters regardless of consequences. Clara copies the Vireaux dispatch in full. Beat: hope and terror sharing a typewriter.

chapters.title: Betrayal in the Motor Pool
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah discovers another household employee has been reporting to the ministry all along—and that his own 'acceptance' was a loyalty test he failed. The file on Thomas has been destroyed. Beat: the trap closing; no clean side left.

chapters.title: Runaway Motorcar
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The Fairweather car's brakes fail on a hill; Jonah survives by instinct and realizes it was no accident. Clara tends his split hands. Beat: fear made physical; love admitted in the space between bandages.

chapters.title: The Archive at Night
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. Jonah and Clara break into the records office to reconstruct the Vireaux file from carbon copies and a chaplain's ledger. Beat: exhilaration—the bystander finally acting on history.

chapters.title: What the Victors Want Forgotten
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The ministry man, Halloway, corners Jonah: publish the letters and Edith will be ruined as a traitor, Thomas posthumously disgraced. He offers Jonah a clean exit and a ticket anywhere. Beat: temptation at its most reasonable.

chapters.title: Edith's Decision
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Edith learns everything—Jonah's reading, Clara's copies, Halloway's offer—and chooses publication over protection. 'I did not march for a peace that lies.' Beat: the moral center holds; Jonah's loyalty vs. truth resolves toward truth.

chapters.title: The Informer
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah confronts the household informer, who breaks down: he has a family and no choices. Jonah lets him go and takes his place in the ministry's ledger. Beat: mercy with a price; Jonah signs his own name to danger.

chapters.title: The Printer on Fetter Lane
chapters.summary: Clara's POV. Clara and a suffragist printer set the letters by hand overnight while police watch the street. Jonah drives decoy routes across London. Beat: breathless, sacred work; the city beautiful and hostile at once.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Halloway's men seize the print shop and most of the copies. Clara is detained for questioning. Jonah, carrying the one hidden set, must decide: flee with the truth or stay to pull Clara out. Beat: the lowest point—love against duty, both losing.

chapters.title: Eleventh Hour
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Armistice morning. Jonah trades the hidden letters to a sympathetic newspaper editor in exchange for his influence on Clara's release, then walks into the ministry to confess everything on the record, dictating his own testimony to a stenographer. Beat: sacrifice as authorship—Jonah puts himself in history.

chapters.title: The Guns Stop
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At eleven o'clock the guns cease. Clara walks free into a city gone mad with bells; Jonah sits in a cold room awaiting consequences. Edith's supplement hits the streets amid the celebration. Beat: triumph and dread in the same breath.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A public inquiry, forced by the published letters, clears Thomas Fairweather. Halloway is quietly retired; Jonah's testimony, inconveniently witnessed, protects him. Beat: justice as paperwork—the book's thesis made flesh.

chapters.title: Letters We Keep
chapters.summary: Clara's POV. Spring, 1919. Jonah and Clara leave London by train, Edith waving from the platform. Clara hands Jonah an unsealed letter—her own—and he reads it openly for the first time. Beat: the reader of letters becomes their author; love chosen over invisibility.
